title: The Western Cape tourism system today

blocks.text: 1.2 The Western Cape tourism system today
The Western Cape's international tourism has recovered to a record, and the system that delivered the recovery runs through five source markets, six summer months and one metro.
Arrivals and recovery

International passenger arrivals at Cape Town International reached 1.44m in FY24/25, against 1.16m in FY19/20, the last pre-pandemic year (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25). Arrivals passed the pre-pandemic peak of 1.19m, set in FY18/19, during FY23/24, when they reached 1.36m (p25). FY25/26 added a further step to 1.57m (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11).

The fall and the climb were both steep. Arrivals dropped to 80,400 in FY20/21 and 378,500 in FY21/22, then returned to 1.07m in FY22/23 (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25). Two-way international passengers reached 2.90m in FY24/25, 29% above FY17/18 (p35), and 3.3m in calendar 2025 inside a total of 11.1m, both up 7% on the year (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p22).

Cape Town's recovery also ran ahead of the national one, so the destination gained share as it recovered. In the first half of 2024 its air arrivals had recovered further against 2019 than South Africa's in eight of the ten largest markets (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p26). The USA stood at 162% and Australia at 172% of their 2019 level (p26).

blocks.title: Three arrivals measures
paras: The 1.44m is ACSA's count of international passengers arriving at Cape Town International in the fiscal year. It is the series this report uses as its recovery baseline and its monitoring base year (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25).

South African Tourism counts tourist arrivals to the province, which the Demand-Side Analysis notes are distinct from airport passenger traffic (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p27). The growth model in Chapter 2 runs from a third series, a 2025 base of 1,498,829 international arrivals (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19).
The deliverables do not reconcile the three, so the report names the measure each time it cites an arrivals figure.

blocks.text: Spend and value

Foreign direct spend in the province rose from R22.7bn in FY2024 to R25.9bn in FY2025, a gain of 14% in one year (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11). The Western Cape earns that spend from a modest share of the national market. Across the four quarters of 2025 it took 16%, 13%, 13% and 16% of South Africa's foreign arrivals and 26%, 20%, 22% and 27% of foreign direct spend (p11).

The gap between the two shares is the province's premium. About a quarter of national spend from about a seventh of arrivals means the average foreign visitor to the Western Cape spends roughly 1.6 times the national average (computed from p11). The province earns about US$890 per international arrival, against US$500 for the rest of South Africa and US$630 for Morocco, though below Kenya's US$1,460 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p15).

More than a quarter of overseas visitors stay between 7 and 21 days, on printed bands that sum to only 48% (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12). Some 5% stay 1 to 2 days, 12% 3 to 4, 14% 7 to 10, 3% 11 to 14, 13% 15 to 21 and 1% other (p12). The Diagnostic prints the same distribution from the 2024 Wesgro Visitor Tracking Survey, in which 52.33% of respondents gave no length of stay, so the bands describe about half the sample (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25).

The modal visitor in the 2024 Wesgro survey spends R1,000 to R2,000 a day, is aged 36 to 50 and travels as a pair (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25). Nearly 40% spend more than R1,000 a day (p27). Self-catering at 17.4% and guesthouses at 9.7% lead accommodation choice, ahead of hotels at 3.6% (p27); together these shares cover under a third of respondents.
Source markets

Five markets supply 63% of overseas arrivals. In 2025 the UK held 19%, Germany 17%, the USA 16%, the Netherlands 7% and France 4%, and the three largest alone held 52% (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p13). The report uses 63%, the sum of the printed shares.

Concentration is not new. On the Cape Town overseas air-arrivals basis for January to August 2024 the same five markets held 61%, with the UK and the USA at 18% each and Germany at 15% (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p29). The growth markets remain small: India supplied about 2.6% of South Africa's overseas tourists in September 2025, the Middle East 2.3% and China 1.4% (p30).

The mature markets also pay the most. Average spend per visitor in 2024 ran from R32,900 for the USA, R26,500 for the UK and R25,600 for Germany down to R8,600 for Namibia and R8,500 for Zimbabwe (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p14). The spread is 3.9 times, and the two regional markets compensate with stability, repeat demand and counter-seasonal volume (p14).

Most of these visitors arrive through someone else's hub. The UAE route carried 222,923 air arrivals into Cape Town in 2025, the UK 158,448, Qatar 126,078, Ethiopia 123,250 and Turkiye 89,090 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p13). The four hub routes through Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa and Istanbul carried 53% of arrivals on the ten largest routes (computed from p13), so the hubs, not the source markets, are the province's working gateways.

blocks.text: Seasonality

Demand peaks in the southern summer. In 2025, 12.7% of overseas visitors travelled in December, 11.5% in January and 11.3% in November, against 6.1% in June and 6.5% in August (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p12). October to March together account for about 62% of the year once the twelve printed shares, which sum to 104.9%, are scaled to 100% [Wesgro Research to confirm the 2025 month-of-travel shares].
The 2024 Wesgro Visitor Tracking Survey, whose monthly shares sum to 100%, gives 61% for October to March and 39% for April to September (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p25, p32).

Supply follows the same curve. June carries 6.4% of 2025 international seat capacity into Cape Town (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"), and Cape Town hotel occupancy was 53% in June 2023 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p34). [Open item: Wesgro Research to supply June 2025 occupancy.] The Diagnostic drew the conclusion early: growth "will depend on improving conversion in Apr-Sep rather than pushing incremental demand into already busy peak months" (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p32).

blocks.caption: Six summer months, October to March, carry between 61% and 62% of overseas visitors' travel in the two years for which month of travel is recorded.

blocks.text: Air and sea access

Ten airlines fly to Cape Town International from Africa, nine from Europe, three from North and South America, two from the Middle East and one from Asia (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p35). The aviation assessment states the gap plainly as "the absence of any direct capacity to any of the Asian markets", India and China included (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Capetown Market"). Twenty-nine international routes serve the airport in 2026 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary").

Cape Town International itself is now the physical ceiling. One runway with no parallel taxiway caps movements at about 30 an hour, and ACSA's programme of about R11.3bn brings relief from about 2032 for the international terminal and about 2033 for the runway (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101 to p103). ACSA's latest schedule shows the realigned runway from December 2026 to December 2029, subject to contract award (ACSA, Q1 2026/27 presentation to the Portfolio Committee on Transport, as reported by Travel News, Aug 2026). The secondary gateways do not change the picture: George, above its design limit at 911,000 passengers in 2025, doubles by 2028 or 2029, with construction from October 2026 (p104, p105; George Herald, Jul 2026), and Cape Winelands Airport targets 2028 with no named carrier (p106, p107).

Cruise has grown without new berth capacity. The province hosted 70, 67 and 79 vessels in the 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 seasons, carrying 144,125, 109,884 and 127,178 passengers (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p37). The Infrastructure Report counts 83 calls at the Cape Town berth in 2024/25, 127,000 passengers and R1.79bn of economic impact (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). [StratEcon 2024/25 cruise report to confirm whether 79 vessels and 83 calls differ by definition.]

Port reliability, not berth space, is the risk. The single berth ran at about 40% of a season capacity of 150 or more calls, and its limits are a 300m ship length and the South-Easter wind (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). The Diagnostic calls the Port of Cape Town "a binding constraint, with congestion and equipment failures affecting export and cruise reliability" (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p34).
Geography of the system

The Cape Metro generates 72.5% of provincial GDPR, a whole-economy share rather than a tourism one (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p39; Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p22). The Cape Winelands follows at 11.2%, the Garden Route at 7.6%, the West Coast at 4.8%, the Overberg at 3% and the Central Karoo at 0.5% (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p42 to p50). The decks date only the Garden Route share, to 2023, while the Metro chart is titled 2024 and the rest carry no year (p39, p42).

Tourism supply is concentrated in the same way. The Infrastructure Report mapped 50,332 tourism assets across the six regions, of which the Metro holds 20,281, or 40.3% (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p2, p23). The Garden Route holds 9,875, the Cape Winelands 7,730, the Overberg 6,176, the West Coast 4,752 and the Central Karoo 1,518 (p34, p45, p56, p67, p78).

Cape Town is the axle of the system, "the province's global shopfront and primary dispersal hub" in the Infrastructure Report's words (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p22). The Diagnostic warns that "any capacity failure in Cape Town quickly becomes a provincial risk, not just a city problem" (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p41). International visitors land there and disperse from there, and readiness falls with each step away: accessibility scores drop from 4.7 in the Metro to 1.0 in the Central Karoo (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88 to p90).

Beyond the Metro the visitor drives. The N2 is "the only continuous inter-regional tourism corridor, creating a single point of failure", and large parts of the province outside the Metro and the Garden Route remain effectively car-only destinations (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p98, p99). The further from Cape Town, the faster the infrastructure falls away (p90).

blocks.text: Rail, roads and utilities

Passenger rail has collapsed as a mode. Trainsets fell from about 110 in 1995 to about 91, pushing some 400,000 commuters onto saturated roads, and congestion in the Metro costs an estimated R2.8bn a year (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p38). Metrorail still runs 460km, five lines and 104 of 121 stations, with 22.7m passenger trips in FY2025, but no line reaches the airport and it is rated functionally unusable for tourism (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p100, p90).

Utilities cap the periphery before demand does. Water scarcity in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route acts as a "hard ceiling" for visitor load, and load shedding raises costs and degrades the experience in peripheral districts (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p38). The airport has no fuel pipeline and depends on road tankers (p38), and the 2017 to 2018 water crisis left a lasting perception of resource pressure (p55).

The remedies are named but not scheduled. The Diagnostic lists four transport enablers, none dated or costed: the Cape Town Integrator, rail restoration and devolution, a high-speed city to airport link and George to Cape Winelands passenger rail (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p38). PRASA's R21.1bn programme and the City's R123bn, 30-year devolution case cover fleet and lines, and neither carries a tourism product or an airport link (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p100).
Institutions

Wesgro runs the demand side of this system through six units: Cape Town Air Access, Cruise Cape Town, the Convention Bureau, Destination Marketing, Research and Tourism (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p7). Around them sit fifteen external organisations, from national agencies and state-owned entities to the province, the City, destination and attraction bodies and private operators (p7). The table below sets out who holds what.

The levers that bind the system sit at different tiers. National government holds visa rules, border compliance, air service agreements and route rights (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). The province holds jobs, inclusion and spatial outcomes, sector development and infrastructure planning; local government holds service delivery, precinct management and events readiness; industry holds route viability, demand generation and product standards (p58).

Alignment across those tiers is thin. Stakeholders described strain at SA Tourism and a lack of fiscal space (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). More than twenty bodies produce tourism data and "there is no single view of visitor behaviour, making strategy reactive rather than predictive" (p56, p57).

Stakeholders say the same. Fifteen of the sixteen organisations interviewed raised industry and government collaboration (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46; the count is of organisations with at least one insight under the theme). The Department of Economic Development named restrictive bilateral air agreements and destination funding materially below peer destinations as high-impact constraints (p24, p25).

blocks.text: None of these constraints is a shortage of visitors. The runway, the single corridor, a rail network visitors cannot use, the thin winter schedule and decision rights split across three tiers all sit outside a marketing budget. The system has recovered; its constraints are now physical and institutional.
